subject: Cooking
title: Raw Honey Isn't a Miracle Cure
description: A quick, practical guide to Raw Honey Isn't a Miracle Cure.

hook.text: Raw honey is marketed as an immune booster, allergy cure, and superfood. Most claims don't hold up.

buildup.text: Honey does have antimicrobial properties — effective topically on wounds. Manuka honey is proven for this.

discovery.text: The allergy claim — that local honey desensitizes you to pollen — has been tested and debunked in controlled trials.

twist.text: Honey is still sugar — about 80% glucose and fructose. Your body processes it the same as table sugar.

climax.text: Raw honey can contain botulism spores — dangerous for infants under 12 months, which is why doctors warn against it.

punchline.text: Honey is a delicious sugar. Not a medicine cabinet.

quiz.question: Why should raw honey never be given to infants under 12 months?

details.summary: Raw honey has mild antibacterial properties and may soothe coughs, but it is not a cure-all. Nutritionally it is primarily sugar with trace amounts of vitamins. Most purported health benefits are exaggerated.
details.whyItMatters: Raw honey commands premium prices based on health claims that science largely does not support. It is a delicious natural sweetener, but treating it as medicine leads to overconsumption of sugar.
takeaways: Raw honey is roughly 80 percent sugar by composition
Some antibacterial properties exist but are modest in dietary use
Medical-grade manuka honey is effective on wounds, not consumed honey

faq.question: Does honey help with seasonal allergies?
faq.answer: The theory that local honey contains pollen that desensitizes allergy sufferers is appealing but unsupported by clinical trials. Bees collect flower pollen, while most allergies are triggered by wind-borne grass and tree pollen. Studies show no significant allergy relief from honey consumption.

faq.question: Is raw honey safe for everyone?
faq.answer: Never give honey to infants under 12 months — it can contain Clostridium botulinum spores that cause infant botulism. For adults and older children, raw honey is safe. Diabetics should treat it as sugar. Despite its natural origin, it raises blood sugar similarly to table sugar.
